Chapter 4: Curiosity Is More Reliable Than Passion
Let’s talk about something that comes up a lot when we think about creative work. People always say you need to be fueled by passion—a kind of fire that drives you to achieve amazing things. But have you ever noticed how passion can be a bit... unpredictable? One moment, you’re all in. The next, that excitement fades, and suddenly you’re left feeling stuck, maybe even a little lost.
Here’s the thing: curiosity is different. It’s steady, and it’s always within reach. Curiosity doesn’t ask you for your soul; it just wants your attention.
Think about someone who feels completely stuck, unsure of what path to take next. You know that familiar advice—just “follow your passion”? But what if you’re not sure where your passion really is? Or what if the things that once lit you up now seem kind of... dull? That’s where curiosity steps in. It doesn’t demand big, dramatic changes. It just whispers little questions: What if I tried this? What would happen if I explored that?
The risks are smaller. The pressure is off. But surprisingly, the rewards can be just as meaningful.
Let me share a quick story. Picture someone who’s spent years in the same job and now feels restless, but has no idea what to do next. Instead of waiting for some huge bolt of inspiration, they start noticing the small things that catch their interest. Maybe a documentary about beekeeping pops up—they get curious, read a book, visit a local apiary, and before long, they’ve picked up a new hobby. None of it was planned. It was just one small step after another, each led by a simple question, not a burning passion.
What most people miss is that curiosity is a much more reliable fuel for creativity. It doesn’t ask for promises or big decisions. All it wants is for you to be open, to follow those tiny threads of interest wherever they might lead. And over time, those little moments of attention can really add up.
Curiosity also has another superpower—it quiets your inner critic. Because when you’re focused on exploring rather than achieving, there’s way less pressure to get everything right. Mistakes? They just become part of the adventure, not proof that you’ve failed. With this mindset, it’s so much easier to try new things, to experiment, and to actually enjoy the process.
Here’s another example: imagine a retiree who, after decades of routine, decides to learn guitar. At first, it’s awkward. Progress is slow. But instead of worrying about becoming a master, they let curiosity lead the way. What if I try this chord? How does this song sound? Each practice session becomes a little adventure—a way to stay engaged and open to whatever comes next.
So many of us wait for passion to strike, thinking creative work has to be huge or life-changing. But in reality, most creative lives are built on simple, repeated acts of curiosity. Being willing to follow a question, to try something new, is often all it takes to keep that creative spark alive.
And over time, you start to see that curiosity is the real guide. It’ll take you to surprising places, open new doors, and keep your work feeling fresh and exciting. Passion might come and go, but curiosity is always there—quietly waiting for you to notice and follow.
